summary:
Sergipe stands under Brazil's national framework and adds a layer of its own. Homosexuality is legal in the state, and Sergipe was among the first states in Brazil, with Mato Grosso do Sul, to write a ban on sexual-orientation discrimination into its state constitution in 1989. On 5 July 2012 the State Judiciary Power issued Provimento nº 06/2012, which regulated same-sex marriage throughout the state.

On 17 December 2025 Sergipe became the first Brazilian state to prohibit discrimination based on gender identity in its own constitution. Constitutional Amendment No. 59, proposed by state representative Linda Brasil (PSOL), amended article 3(II) of the State Constitution to guarantee state-level protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, with violators subject to punishment by law effective upon promulgation.

Since 2025 Sergipe has allowed individuals to change the gender marker on their documents to non-binary.

On 28 August 2025 the Court of Justice of Sergipe announced gender-neutral restrooms at the Palácio da Justiça in Aracaju, operating on the ground, 1st and 8th floors and usable by any person regardless of gender identity. The same announcement mandates that in all Sergipe judiciary units male and female bathrooms be used in a way that respects each person's gender identity, and requires gender-equity demands to be built into all new constructions and renovations.

Restrictive initiatives sit alongside these protections. On 1 December 2020 state representative Rodrigo Valadares (UNIÃO) tabled a bill to prohibit the use and teaching of gender-neutral language in Sergipe's public and private schools and in state public offices, requiring traditional Portuguese in schools, official notices and public offices.
tangentialFactors:
A Brazilian law-firm guide for expatriates (OAB/SP, updated April 2026) reports that enforcement of the country's LGBTQ protections is uneven: major cities such as São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Brasília are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights. The guide names no Sergipe municipality, so the degree of variation between Aracaju and the state's interior is not sourced.

Sergipe's own record runs in both directions within a five-year window: a 2020 bill aimed at gender-neutral language in schools and state offices, followed in 2025 by a constitutional amendment against gender-identity discrimination, a non-binary document marker and gender-neutral restrooms in the state judiciary.
localsOnly:
The Federal University of Sergipe created quotas for trans people in undergraduate courses on 17 November 2025, an admissions benefit that reaches residents and students rather than visitors.

The bill tabled on 1 December 2020 by Rodrigo Valadares would bind state schools, state public offices and official notices; its practical effect, if enacted, would fall on residents and the state administration.

Sergipe's 1989 constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination and the amendment of 17 December 2025 give residents a state-level protection against discrimination on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with violators subject to punishment by law.
outOfScopeNotes:
The fate of the gender-neutral-language bill tabled on 1 December 2020 is unresolved: the inventory records its introduction only, and whether it advanced, stalled or was defeated is not sourced.

Whether the non-binary gender marker available in Sergipe since 2025 applies to state-issued documents alone or reaches federally issued documents is not specified in the sources.

No Sergipe-specific incident of anti-trans violence, police conduct or discriminatory refusal of service appears in the inventory. The enforcement record under Constitutional Amendment No. 59, promulgated 17 December 2025, is unverified.

Whether the judiciary's restroom mandate extends beyond court buildings to other public facilities in Sergipe is not sourced.
